concepts.name: Ideal pipeline performance
facts: N instructions take M+N-1 cycles in an M-stage pipeline.
This assumes no bubbles and one completion per cycle after filling.

evidence.quote:
¡ Perfect Pipeline
¡ One instruction completes per cycle after filling 
the pipeline.
¡ No bubbles and maximum throughput.
¡ For N instructions and M stages:
¡ Total Cycles = M + N – 1
¡ Average throughput
= N / (M + N - 1) instructions per cycle
¡ Instruction throughput per second                    
Frequency * N / (M + N - 1)

concepts.name: Amdahl's law
facts: For a fixed problem size, S(p)=1/((1-f)+f/p).
f is the parallelizable fraction.
The serial fraction limits maximum speedup.

evidence.quote:
Performance Models
¡ When problem size is fixed, even a small serial fraction caps total speedup
Amdahl's Law: The Serial Fraction Wins
S(p) = 1 / ((1 - f) + f / p)
f: parallelizable fraction
1 - f: serial fraction
p: number of processors / threads
NUMERICAL INTUITION
f = 0.90
max speedup -> 10x
f = 0.99
max speedup -> 100x
FIXED PROBLEM SIZE
serial
parallelizable work
More processors squeeze the blue part, but 
the purple serial part remains.

Optimization #5: Speculative Execution
¡ Prediction for next instructions
¡
Issue risky instructions on the chance of considerable benefits.
¡ Benefit
¡
Quick completion --- low latency
¡
Keep deep pipeline busy --- high throughput
¡ Cost
¡
Wrong-path work wastes energy and cycles.
¡
Recovery penalty grows with pipeline depth and speculation window.

¡
The compiler resolves user’s codes and find the 
branches that would not be taken.
¡
Remove corresponding instructions to avoid 
control hazards.
¡ Dynamic Branch Prediction
¡
Learn branch behavior autonomously, no 
compiler analysis or profiling
¡
Adapt to changing branch behavior
